Feasibility means implementability with current resources and technology. FlexMind ideas scored higher than ChatGPT baseline ideas on feasibility (p < .05). Figure 6 supplies plotted means and standard-error bars, but no numerical arm means or SDs for this dimension; do not estimate those from the bars.

corrections.source_says: Record that four domain experts rated anonymized ideas blind to condition, with two experts per task. The two ratings on each dimension were averaged per idea, and their geometric mean formed overall quality; novelty and value are dimension scores. For overall quality, also note the additional chain-length analysis in Table 3: two submitted ideas per participant per condition were randomly sampled, and the model includes condition, idea chain length, their interaction, and a participant random intercept. This is another analysis of the same outcome, not random assignment of people.
corrections.quote: For each idea, we averaged the two raters’ scores on each dimension and then computed the geometric mean to yield the overall idea-quality score used in analysis.
corrections.locator: PDF p. 8, Section 4.1.4, Idea Quality Evaluation; pp. 9–10, Section 4.1.6(2); p. 13, Table 3.

confirmed: The source is the 30-page arXiv:2509.21685v2 dated 29 Sep 2025; the title and author list match, and Appendix 8 is included on PDF pp. 21–30 (p. 1 version line and authors; pp. 21–30 appendix). The entire markdown, including references and appendices, was read.

S1 includes 20 analyzed people completing both conditions, not 40 independent people; the two arm counts of 20 refer to the same sample (PDF p. 7, Sections 4.1.2–4.1.3; p. 10, Section 5.1; p. 12, Figures 7–8).

Counterbalancing is stated, but random assignment of people or condition order is not. The explicit random sampling concerns ideas for rubric calibration and chain-length analysis; it does not establish a randomized people study (PDF p. 7, Section 4.1.3; p. 8, Section 4.1.4; pp. 9–10, Section 4.1.6). Accordingly, has_randomized_people_study=false means not established by this source, not proven non-random allocation.

S1 design_class=other, eligibility.core=no, criterion_1=unclear, criterion_2=not_met, criterion_3=met, and context_class=none are supported: order randomization is unstated, only 20 people were analyzed, and blinded experts scored submitted ideas (PDF pp. 7–8, Sections 4.1.2–4.1.4; p. 12, Figures 7–8).

Both controlled-study conditions used o4-mini. Participants completed laundry-water and walking-while-texting design tasks for 30 minutes each in a 90-minute remote session (PDF p. 7, Sections 4.1–4.1.3).
S1-O1 and the one-line finding correctly report FlexMind M=3.18, SD=0.63 versus baseline M=2.59, SD=0.65, with Welch’s t-test p<0.001 (PDF p. 10, Section 5.1).

S1-O1 and the one-line finding correctly report the Table 2 condition coefficient: 0.473, SE=0.115, z=4.10, p<0.0001, 95% CI [0.247, 0.699]. This is an idea-quality difference on the 1–5 scale, with a participant random intercept, not a standardized effect (PDF p. 9, Section 4.1.6(1); p. 11, Table 2).
The S1-O2 novelty and S1-O3 value reported strings correctly say FlexMind scored higher, p<.001 for each (PDF p. 11, Figure 6 caption).

The idea-quality analysis unit is the submitted idea, with expert ratings aggregated per idea; participant counts must remain distinct from idea and rating counts (PDF p. 8, Section 4.1.4; p. 11, Figure 6 and Table 2).

S2 is a separate six-person expert study using FlexMind without a baseline on self-chosen tasks, in 60-minute remote sessions. Its reported analysis is qualitative and self-reported, with no independently scored output-quality outcome and no tree-based metrics computed for this sample (PDF p. 10, Sections 4.2.1–4.2.5; p. 22, Table 9).

Figure 9 diversity ratings are self-reports, and Figure 8 measures exposure to solutions; neither establishes a scored across-people diversity outcome (PDF p. 7, Section 4.1.3; p. 12, Figures 8–9; p. 14, Section 5.3).

This is an empirical paper with a controlled user study and a separate expert study, not a synthesis; pooled-study counts and pooled estimates are inapplicable (PDF p. 7, Section 4; p. 10, Section 4.2).
summary: The 20-person counterbalanced study remains ineligible for the core dataset, and random assignment of condition order is not stated. The reported effect statistics match the PDF, but the form omits feasibility, output-count discrepancies, outcome metadata, and Toyota Research Institute involvement.
